problem: The numbers and the description contradict each other and the chapter's own definition of φ. With φ = (F/A) ÷ (F/A)stoich, a value of 0.85 is a lean mixture (85 % of the stoichiometric fuel-air ratio), not rich. So "φ = 0.85 to 1.0, that is, slightly rich to stoichiometric" is wrong, and it also clashes with the exam trap that says knock is worst at a slightly rich mixture. Standard textbooks place maximum knock on the rich side of stoichiometric.
fix: Knock tendency is highest for slightly rich mixtures, about φ = 1.05 to 1.15, that is, an air-fuel ratio of roughly 13:1, close to but richer than stoichiometric. Leaner mixtures (φ < 0.9) and very rich mixtures (φ > 1.2) both knock less.

where: Section 1, first line of mixture strength paragraph
problem: "Mixture strength is the ratio of fuel to air" is loose. Mixture strength normally means how the actual fuel-air ratio compares with the stoichiometric one, which is exactly the equivalence ratio defined in the next sentence, so the sentence is circular.
fix: Mixture strength tells how far the actual fuel-air ratio is from the chemically correct one. It is written as the equivalence ratio φ.
